citation.title: The size of national delegations and the need for attendance regulation at climate conferences
citation.venue_or_publisher: Ökologisches Wirtschaften 1.2016 (31), pp. 12-13 (section 'Aktuelle Berichte'; IÖW and oekom verlag)
citation.type: Published journal version (PDF, 2 pages), short report in the 'Aktuelle Berichte' section, under a CC BY-NC-ND licence

question: Whether the growing size of national delegations at UNFCCC COPs, and how countries select delegates, serves climate decision-making; argues for guidelines on delegation composition and attendance.
data: No data set or period of its own is described. It cites other studies (Schroeder et al. 2012; Schroeder/Lovell 2012; Neeff 2013) and gives one attendance figure for COP21.
method: Short commentary. No classification, counting or coding method is described.

proxies.indicator: Delegates listed in the official list of participants with no affiliation given
proxies.quote: The official list of participants for various sessions shows some names of the delegates without any information on the affiliations.

proxies.concept: Delegation composition by type of professional
proxies.indicator: Share of delegation from business associations, academics, government officials or political leaders (as reported from the cited studies; the article does not give its own coding scheme)
proxies.quote: For an instance, Brazil sends more from business associations, while Russia prefers to send more academics and researchers.

findings.claim: Countries differ in the kind of professionals they put in their delegations; Brazil is given as sending more business association delegates (attributed to Schroeder et al. 2012).
findings.quote: For an instance, Brazil sends more from business associations, while Russia prefers to send more academics and researchers.

findings.claim: G8 delegations grew while those of small developing countries declined (attributed to Schroeder et al. 2012).
findings.quote: The G8 countries have increased the number of delegates they send; in contrast, participation from small, developing countries has been in decline

findings.claim: In some countries political leaders make up about a fifth of the delegation; the authors say the share of academics and officials has been declining in some countries.
findings.quote: In some cases, political leaders form around 20 % of the national delegation.

findings.claim: The UNFCCC has limited observer organisations' nominations since 2010, but attendance still grew.
findings.quote: the organizer since 2010 has restricted the observer organizations to nominate representatives.

findings.claim: COP21 in Paris had 36,276 participants including media and observers, well above the predicted 14,000 to 28,000.
findings.quote: a total of 36,276 participants, including media and observer organizations, have attended the COP21 in Paris

findings.claim: Authors' recommendation (argument, not a finding): the UNFCCC should issue guidelines on delegation composition that include the private sector among other groups, with a competency questionnaire for delegates.
findings.quote: the UNFCCC may initiate guidelines on the composition to ensure a poised group of participants that would include experts from academia and research, private sector, NGOs and development organizations

limitations.point: Very short commentary with no data, method or classification scheme of its own; the 'business' and 'political leader' categories are not defined; claims on delegation composition rest on cited secondary studies and a few country examples.
No mention of fossil fuel links, lobbying, conflict of interest or undue influence; private sector appears only as one group to be included in balanced delegations.
Page 2 contains an advertisement for a book (Nachhaltige Unternehmensentwicklung im Mittelstand); it holds no instructions to a reader or AI.
